vignette: Elias sits across from me, his hands resting on his knees, fingers tracing the seam of his jeans. He is forty-six, European-born, and has not worn a uniform in seven years. The call that pulls him out of that life unfolds on a Tuesday in late October. A routine traffic stop on a rain-slicked overpass fractures into a confrontation. A suspect reaches toward his waistband. Elias draws his sidearm. The gunshot echoes off the concrete pillars. It takes three seconds. It takes the rest of his life to process. In the immediate aftermath, the sound of backfiring cars locks his chest. He starts sleeping with the bedroom door propped open, a heavy oak chair wedged under the knob. His wife, Sarah, notices how his eyes track the ceiling corners before they finally settle on her face. He stops talking about the call. He tells himself it is protocol, part of the necessary decompression, but the silence stretches until it feels like a second skin. He returns to civilian life as a graphic designer, trading patrol shifts for screen glare and client revisions. At first, the work acts as an anchor. Composition offers order. Layers hide or reveal on command. But the precision becomes a trap. When he opens a design file to map a client’s brand identity, his cursor hovers over color palettes. He finds himself avoiding deep reds, then blacks, then any layout that requires sharp, high-contrast typography. The studio monitors grow too bright, too exposing. He starts wearing blue-light glasses indoors, claiming it is his eyes, not the screens. Deadlines pile up. He works late, moving his mouse in tight, controlled circles, convinced that if he just finds the perfect alignment, the internal noise will finally quiet. Now, Elias measures his days in near-misses. He takes different routes to the grocery store, checking rearview mirrors at every intersection. When the neighbor’s lawn mower cuts too loud or a car door slams in the parking garage, his breath catches before his brain catches up. He wakes at 2:14 a.m. consistently. He lies still, counting the floorboards between his bed and the front door. Sarah sleeps on her side of the mattress, her breathing steady, but he flinches when her hand drifts toward him in his sleep. He loves her fiercely, which is exactly why he keeps his stories locked behind a quiet, practiced neutrality. He cooks dinner every night, chopping vegetables with methodical rhythm, grounding himself in the sharp thud of the knife against the board. He still designs. His work remains technically flawless, but the creative spark flattens into something functional, safe. He tells clients he is streamlining his process, which is a gentle lie. In session, he watches my hands when they move across the table. He remembers the weight of the trigger guard, the smell of wet asphalt and cordite, the way the suspect’s knees buckled. He knows these memories are real. He also knows they live inside him like unopened files, waiting for the wrong directory to launch them. He finishes his coffee, sets the cup down carefully, and asks if we can talk about how to make his designs feel less like armor. I nod. The silence between us is not empty. It is full of everything he has not yet named.
